summary: Defines common mechanisms for managing asynchronously produced alerts in a way consistent with current network management protocols. It is an Experimental document.

plainLanguage.summary: Devices can call out when something goes wrong. This tries ways to make sure those calls are organized.

questions: how to manage asynchronous alerts in network management
how do polled logged alerts work
subtitle: Managing how often devices send alerts to avoid overwhelming network managers.

tldr.problem: Network management must balance two needs: polling for status generates heavy network traffic and slow detection of problems, but asynchronous alerts can flood a manager with data when many failures occur at once, preventing effective management.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes two mechanisms: a feedback-based throttle that automatically stops sending alerts when their rate exceeds a limit, and a polled log of alerts that avoids relying on alert delivery while reducing polling traffic.
tldr.outcome: Management stations can use alerts for rapid fault detection while guaranteeing delivery of important information and avoiding alert storms that would disable the manager itself.

facts.label: Two core techniques
facts.value: Feedback-based throttling and polled, logged alerts

facts.label: Log entry wraparound
facts.value: alertId wraps at 2^32; oldest entry replaced when log is full

today: RFC 1224 is an Experimental protocol from May 1991 that defines mechanisms for managing alerts in network management systems. It works within existing management frameworks like SNMP and CMOT without modifying the core protocols.

sections.title: The Polling vs. Alert Tradeoff
sections.content:
Network managers have two ways to learn about problems. Polling means asking devices "Are you okay?" repeatedly. This guarantees the manager detects failures, does not overload devices, and requires no configuration of where alerts go. But polling many devices and parameters takes time and network bandwidth, so managers detect problems slowly (perhaps minutes after they occur).

Alerts are unsolicited messages sent when a problem is detected. They provide real-time notification and generate minimal network traffic in healthy systems. But when a cascade of failures occurs, a device may send alerts so rapidly that they saturate the network, preventing the manager from receiving critical information or even issuing commands to stop the alert flood. Additionally, alerts can be lost if the network or the failing device cannot deliver them.
sections.plainLanguage: Polling is like a teacher checking each student's desk every few minutes. Alerts are like students raising their hands when they need help. Both have problems: checking takes a long time, and everyone raising hands at once is chaos.

sections.title: Feedback-Based Alert Throttling
sections.content:
The first technique uses a sliding window limit (called the "pin") to automatically control alert rate. Two MIB objects define the limit: maxAlertsPerTime (the maximum number of alerts allowed) and windowTime (the time period in seconds to measure over). A third object, alertsEnabled, is a Boolean flag set by the manager.

When the device generates alerts, it tracks the timestamps of the most recent ones. If the number of alerts sent in the past windowTime seconds reaches maxAlertsPerTime, the device automatically sets alertsEnabled to FALSE and sends a single alert of type alertsDisabled. This stops all further alerts from being sent. The manager, upon receiving alertsDisabled, must set alertsEnabled back to TRUE to resume receiving alerts, providing the required positive feedback.
sections.plainLanguage: You can say "Do not send me more than 10 warnings in 3 seconds." If the device hits that limit, it sends one message saying "I am stopping alerts now" and shuts up until you tell it to start again.

sections.title: Polled, Logged Alerts
sections.content:
The second technique stores alerts in a log table on the managed device and lets the manager poll for them, combining the reliability of polling with the efficiency of alert-driven management. As local alerts are generated, each one is added to the alert log with a unique alert ID and a copy of the alert data. The log has a maximum size; when full, the oldest entry is replaced.

The manager polls a single MIB object to learn if any new alerts exist. When it finds an alert ID, it can retrieve the complete alert data for that ID. The manager can acknowledge (remove) alerts from the log, preventing their loss if the manager cannot be reached. This way, a manager polling once per minute learns of all alerts that occurred, with a maximum detection delay of about 30 seconds on average.
sections.plainLanguage: The device writes down all the problems in a notebook. You check the notebook once a minute. You read what happened, and mark it as checked so you remember what you saw.

sections.title: Compatibility with SNMP and CMOT
sections.content:
Both techniques work within the existing SNMP and CMOT management protocols. The feedback mechanism uses SNMP traps (the alertsDisabled trap) and SNMP GET/SET operations on the configuration MIB objects. For polled, logged alerts, the manager uses SNMP GET NEXT to iterate through the log table by alert ID, retrieves alert data with SNMP GET, and uses SNMP SET to delete entries.

CMOT implementations use equivalent operations: CMOT EVENT for alerts, CMOT GET and SET for configuration, and CMOT DELETE to remove log entries. No changes to the underlying management protocols are required; the techniques simply define a standard set of MIB objects that agents can implement.
sections.plainLanguage: Both SNMP and CMOT are ways managers talk to devices. These techniques just add some new things to ask about and new messages that devices can send, using the existing conversation method.

sections.title: Combined Approach and Multi-Manager Environments
sections.content:
The RFC suggests using both techniques together: feedback throttling prevents alert floods during failures, while polled, logged alerts ensure important information is not lost if the asynchronous delivery fails. During normal operation, the manager gets real-time alerts; during alert storms, feedback disables the flood and the log preserves a history.

In networks with multiple managers, different managers can see different alert states. Managers can specify different feedback thresholds and independently acknowledge alerts from the log, allowing each management domain to focus on its own priorities. Some implementations may use proxy managers that aggregate alerts from many devices and apply feedback on behalf of multiple subscribers.
sections.plainLanguage: You can use both methods at once: if something goes really wrong, you stop the shouting and check the notebook instead. If multiple people are managing the network, each one can keep their own notebook.

left.title: Polling
left.desc: Manager asks periodically; always learns the truth but causes traffic.

right.title: Alerts
right.desc: Device notifies immediately; minimal traffic when normal but can flood when problems occur.
